title: Defensible first-century prices, wages and coin conversions for the Chronomap economy
question: What do papyri, coin finds and numismatic catalogues (RPC, Hendin), Josephus, the Mishnah and peer-reviewed economic histories establish about daily wages, bread and wheat prices, clothing, rent and the purchasing power of the denarius in first-century CE Judaea and the eastern Mediterranean, and which conversion conventions are defensible: 1 denarius = 16 asses after c. 141 BCE, 1 talent = 6000 denarii/drachmas, and what is the mine? Specifically, can the Mishnah's 200-zuz poverty line, the 2-denarius inn payment (Lk 10:35), Antipas' 200-talent tribute (Ant. 17:318) and the 'two sparrows for an as' (Mt 10:29) be converted into a consistent price scale, and where must the Chronomap show a range rather than a point value?
why_now: The money file was revised on 21.11.2026 to provide a source-backed basis for the Chronomap game economy, but it still lists open points on first-century bread and wheat prices and on the mine/talent conversion; the same values feed the Chronomap economy and the Academy material.
real_world_anchor: First-century CE prices, wages and coin conversions in Roman Judaea and the eastern Mediterranean: papyri, coin hoards, RPC/Hendin catalogues, Josephus, and the Mishnah.
novelty_reason: No previous topic covers ancient prices, wages or coinage. The prior Georgist land-value-taxation topic concerns modern LVT and outer-space property law, not Roman-period market prices or numismatic conversion conventions.
